item.title: Images Emerge From Quake-Battered Colombia
item.description:
Shortly after 7:30 on Monday morning, the most powerful earthquake to hit Colombia in a decade sent people fleeing for safety as buildings teetered and then fell.

The epicenter was in a less populous rural area off the Pacific Coast, potentially blunting its effect, but even so, by midafternoon, Colombian officials were reporting that at least 111 people had been confirmed dead.

More than 1,500 residential buildings were damaged, they said, some of them irreparably. At least 20 buildings collapsed in the city of Cali, trapping people inside, according to its mayor.

Eighteen health centers and dozens of schools were also damaged, and air service to more than half a dozen cities was suspended.

item.title: Journalism and Paywalls
item.description:
When we first launched this newsletter almost a year ago, we did something unique: Not only was the newsletter free to read, but all the news stories we linked to were free as well.

We wanted to make sure our readers around the world — you all — could get to know our journalism before we ask you to support us. That time has now come. The newsletter will remain free. But the free access to links inside will be limited to a select few a day.

Some of you have written in, surprised and sometimes annoyed at the prospect of hitting the paywall. I get it. So in today’s newsletter, I want to explain why we need people who can afford it to pay for our journalism. Many of you already do. Thank you.

You may have heard that the phone records of several colleagues were recently subpoenaed by the Trump administration. In some cases, federal agents showed up at the homes of Times journalists demanding their testimony before a grand jury.

The aim was to force them to disclose the names of confidential sources who had informed their reporting about the security shortcomings of President Trump’s new Air Force One jet, a present from Qatar. They continued to cover the story despite threats from the F.B.I.

This isn’t the first time we’ve had to defend ourselves against a government unhappy about the probing eye of investigative journalism — and it won’t be the last. Trump and his campaign have already filed three lawsuits against The New York Times. Unlike some other outlets that settled, we stood our ground. So far we’ve won every time, though some litigation is still pending.

This increasingly hostile environment for independent reporting in the United States and elsewhere in the world has made our job much harder. My colleagues have had to find new ways to report in the face of limited access, increased surveillance and more fearful sources.

Our publisher A.G. Sulzberger gave a speech last year, encouraging journalists to keep reporting “without fear or favor.” For The New York Times that means spending more on safety, security and litigation than ever before — nearly 10 times more than a decade ago, he said.

We are also consulting with our lawyers more than in the past to make sure we’re not inadvertently exposing ourselves to legal risks.

It all leads to a hard truth: Independent journalism has become a lot more challenging and expensive to produce. But that’s also what makes it a lot more important.

A world hostile to journalism

In more and more places, journalists face arrest or violence for reports that challenge the government.

We’ve had a journalist expelled from China. Israel has barred foreign journalists from operating freely in Gaza for almost three years now.

But my colleagues are still reporting on those places, and others, because we believe their stories need to be told.

The New York Times puts journalists on the ground in more than 150 countries. That’s how Kim Barker could tell The World about her experience on the Ukrainian front lines. And Abdi Latif Dahir reported for us on the streets of Tehran during the former Iranian leader’s recent funeral. And Jack Nicas went to Cuba to cover its attempts to survive during a U.S. oil blockade.

They are our — and your — eyes and ears on the ground. They are what hopefully makes The New York Times and this newsletter valuable to you. Paying them fairly and keeping them safe is expensive. Last year, The Times published nearly half a million original pieces of journalism — articles, photos, videos, podcasts — at a cost of more than $2 billion, according to A.G.

The A.I. revolution

An already very challenging environment for news organizations is not getting any easier. Following the internet revolution, we bled ad revenues. The U.S. lost more than 3,000 newspapers over the last two decades.

Now we’re into the A.I. revolution, and subscription revenues could be next in line. A.G. recently wrote an essay (available for free!) explaining how A.I. companies pose a threat. They’re taking our journalism to train their models without paying for it, then offer it up as their own instead of sending potential subscribers back to us.

“Tech giants strip-mine news websites without permission or compensation,” he wrote. “They repackage these stolen goods as their own, siphoning off the audiences and revenue that otherwise would go to the news organizations that created this work.”

The New York Times was the largest source of proprietary data in a major dataset used to train many different models, A.G. said.

That’s why we’re currently suing OpenAI and Microsoft. But as A.G. noted, “lawsuits are slow and expensive — ours has already stretched two-and-a-half years and cost over $20 million. As A.I. companies are doubtless aware, most news organizations lack the resources to go to court to enforce their rights.”

All this is to say — there is an inherent tension in our mission to produce independent quality journalism and get that journalism before as many eyes as possible.

I, too, wish we could make it all available for free. But I hope I’ve explained why that’s not possible. So if you value our journalism, please subscribe to The New York Times. In the meantime, rest assured this newsletter will still be in your inbox every morning for free.

The magnitude 7.4 quake shook several major cities in western Colombia, including the capital, Bogotá; Cali; and Medellín. At least 111 people were killed, and the death toll appeared likely to rise.

At least 20 buildings collapsed in Cali, trapping people inside, according to the city’s mayor. Officials warned of aftershocks. Follow our live coverage.

Lily Kuo and Callie Holtermann, two Times reporters, recently noticed the same nostalgia trend on opposite sides of the world. In both China and the U.S., many young people are interested in the early internet: Microsoft WordArt, hyper-saturated websites, rotating cursors, Windows graphics.

“If there is too much rain, it will destroy the crop,” one farmer said. “If there is no rain, that will also be destructive.” He added: “It seems that nature is no longer on our side.” Read more about Pakistan’s chile farmers.

item.title: Russian Court Bars Country’s Only Antiwar Party From Running for Parliament
item.description:
Russia’s only antiwar party, Yabloko, has been barred from running in next month’s parliamentary elections, the latest sign that the Kremlin will not tolerate any political forces that question its determination to continue fighting in Ukraine.

The Supreme Court, in a hastily called hearing on Monday, upheld a lawsuit seeking to strike Yabloko from the ballot for the Sept. 18 election.

Kirill Goncharov, head of the party’s Moscow chapter, said Yabloko had been bracing for that decision.

“We were aware that the more popular we were getting, the more trouble we’re creating for the Kremlin,” he told The New York Times shortly after the verdict. “People want peace, freedom and a life without fear — people want what this party represents.”

Unless its appeal is upheld within the next five days, Yabloko will not be able to run in the elections.

The decision is yet another example of the Russian authorities’ trying to sideline antiwar voices ahead of an election that is widely seen to be sewn up for President Vladimir V. Putin’s governing United Russia party.

Even apparent fringe threats to the Kremlin’s power have stoked fear within the political elite about the risks of allowing any pluralism during wartime.

In the run-up to the presidential election in 2024, a relatively unknown antiwar candidate, Boris B. Nadezhdin, was barred from running as his candidacy began to gain steam. He was also arrested. He fled the country last week as he prepared to run in the parliamentary election.

Yabloko is the only Russian political party that did not support the war and openly called for a cease-fire. It has been criticized, however, for failing to clearly condemn Mr. Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Such statements have landed hundreds of Russians in prison on criminal charges linked to war censorship laws.

Yabloko’s short-lived campaign in recent weeks have attracted young voters who took to social media to profess their love of apples — “yabloko” in Russian. Danya Milokhin, a singer with a huge following among Russian teenagers, posted a supportive video over the weekend.

Before the verdict, several hundred people, mostly young Russians, showed up at the Supreme Court on Monday morning to cheer on the party, singing “Yabloko” on the steps of the building after most of them were not allowed in.

The case for striking Yabloko off the ballot was started by Rodina, an obscure nationalist party whose leader, Aleksei Zhuravlyov, accused Yabloko of “working for the West” and betraying Russia by opposing the war in Ukraine.

A trial that would normally take at least a few weeks to set up was scheduled for Monday, the next working day after the claim was filed.

Rodina’s representatives on Monday asked the court to disqualify Yabloko over several alleged instances of copyright infringement, including quoting from a Soviet-era children’s song in an interview of the party’s founder and failing to display credits for a photo on its webpage.

None of the copyright owners, including the newspaper and the heirs of a Soviet composer, voiced any issues with Yabloko.

Even the pro-Kremlin observer Sergei Markov, a political scientist, on Monday said on social media he “cannot get his head around” the accusations.

The lawsuit also said Yabloko should not be allowed to run as it had been encroaching on “Russia’s territorial integrity” by calling for an end of the war.

In response to the claim, Nikolai Rybakov, the party’s leader, cited in court on Monday Mr. Putin’s recent remarks saying that Russia was pursuing peace talks.

As the judge announced the verdict late Monday evening, Grigory A. Yavlinsky, Yabloko’s co-founder and former longtime leader, said in a statement that Russia’s “political system has exposed itself by barring Yabloko from running.”

Russian society wants “peace and freedom way more than the authorities thought,” he said.

Yabloko, which has not held a party-list seat in Russia’s lower house of Parliament, known as the Duma, since 2003, has become an unlikely magnet for antiwar Russians at home and abroad after election officials gave it the green light last month to run. Its 43-word election manifesto focused on two things: peace and freedom.

Allowing Yabloko on the ballot could make the party a protest vote at a time when much of Russian society is exasperated with the war and wants it to end, analysts say. The Kremlin apparently does not want to take even that risk.

Some of the party’s most prominent members have already been disqualified: Mr. Rybakov, the party leader, cannot run because of a court decision punishing him for posting a photo of Aleksei A. Navalny, the Russian opposition leader who died in a penal colony in 2024. Maxim Kruglov, deputy chairman of the party, was sentenced to seven years in prison in June over a 2022 social media post calling out what experts have described as Russian war crimes in the suburbs of Kyiv in the first weeks of the invasion.

Yabloko has also been barred from fielding candidates in St. Petersburg and Karelia, where it has been historically strong in the local legislatures.

Years before Yabloko was accused of submitting to the Kremlin’s war censorship, elements of the Russian opposition have accused it of being too soft on Mr. Putin’s increasingly authoritarian regime.

But most of these critics rallied around Yabloko and called on their supporters to vote for the party in the upcoming election.

Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Mr. Navalny, last week said she and her allies would “set aside all disagreements and help” Yabloko at the polls.

Ms. Navalnaya, commenting on Monday’s ruling, said that “the Kremlin got spooked” by Yabloko’s growing popularity. She called on her supporters to “vote for any party other than United Russia.”

item.title: A.C. Vests and UV Parasols: East Asia Deploys Heat-Fighting Gadgets
item.description:
Stroll through Tokyo on a summer day and you’ll see hand-held fans everywhere. But the light-blue one that Eimi Nakayama was holding on a recent afternoon was a more high-tech variety. Outfitted with a small metal plate that runs on the same science behind semiconductors, it uses electrical currents to generate a chill.

The sensation is “kind of like holding a cold drink against your neck,” said Ms. Nakayama, a 20-year-old university student. “Maybe because of the plate, the air flow feels a bit cooler, too.”

The product has lately been sweeping through cities in East Asia, where a deadly heat wave this month has led to canceled baseball games in South Korea and a new meteorological term in Japan: kokushobi, or “cruel heat day.”

East Asia’s summers are becoming hotter and longer, and such “personal cooling” has become a ubiquitous part of daily life. A market once dominated by inexpensive hand-held fans now includes a growing array of more sophisticated products, from air-conditioned apparel to cooling sprays that claim to lower your body temperature within seconds.

Sales of cooling products are soaring, and employers and governments increasingly see them as a necessity rather than a luxury.

As in Japan, the market for such products in South Korea has grown dramatically over the past two years, said Lee Joo-young, an expert in the relationship between clothing and thermal environments at Seoul National University. She said a major factor is that motors and batteries have become cheaper and more effective, making powerful new cooling products accessible.

In Japan, the birthplace of the fan-cooled jacket — invented by Hiroshi Ichigaya, a former Sony electrical engineer, in 2004 — the online market for “heat countermeasure” products has expanded more than sixfold since 2020, according to Rakuten, one of the country’s biggest e-commerce platforms. It now lists roughly 800,000 products in that category.

Mr. Ichigaya’s invention has since evolved considerably. One apparel company recently introduced a vest studded with the same metal plates now appearing on hand-held fans.

But these gadgets are no longer just aimed at consumers looking for quick relief during their commutes. Increasingly, they are becoming part of how governments and employers are adapting to extreme heat.

Chinese delivery platform Meituan is piloting “air-con jackets” — another spin on Mr. Ichigaya’s invention — for its delivery workers in Chongqing, a city in the country’s southwest. In Hubei Province in central China, the state-owned power company has equipped some of its workers with waist-mounted mini fans.

In Japan, the Ministry of the Environment and Tokyo’s metropolitan government have promoted parasols as an effective way to reduce heat stress, while some South Korean municipalities have been outfitting their street cleaners with neon cooling vests.

In South Korea, the need for such technologies is especially great on farms, said Kim In-soo, a researcher at the country’s National Institute of Agricultural Sciences. He recently designed his own cooling vest for greenhouse workers that is being piloted at 350 farms around the country.

“Greenhouses are one of the worst places to be during a heat wave,” he said. “It’s hot and humid and a lot of the work is time-sensitive harvesting that can’t be stopped at will.”

The vest, which relies on a technology known as a “vortex tube,” is hooked up to a compressor that shoots cold, dry air into thin tubes, which then distribute it across the skin through tiny perforations running throughout the vest.

Seo Hye-young, the 35-year-old founder of a South Korean start-up that sells cooling neck bands online, has built a business around the growing appetite for cooling products, a trend she first noticed a few years ago.

At around $35 apiece, Ms. Seo’s product — a thick, squishy collar filled with coolant — is among the pricier options, but promises shorter freezing times and “explosive” cooling effects. She is on track to sell around 60,000 units this year.

“But it got so hot so quickly this year that we’re struggling to keep up with the sudden demand,” she said.

The race to beat the heat has spawned more unusual inventions. In Japan, one company has developed a human-sized refrigerated booth that offers quick relief at construction sites, universities and evacuation shelters for natural disasters. Across East Asia, manufacturers are serving up solar-powered fan hats, hands-free parasols and air-conditioned pet houses, among other specialized devices.

But Ms. Lee, the professor, said cooling gadgets should not be treated as a cure-all.

“When the temperature is above 33 degrees Celsius or so, fans just blow hot air onto your skin,” she said. And the cooling neck bands? They lose their chill too quickly to make a big difference, she added.

For most people, she said, the low-tech options are often most effective: drinking cold beverages; keeping your feet — among the body’s most notorious heat-trappers — uncovered and cool; and shielding yourself from the sun with parasols, many of which now have black undersides that block UV rays.

Among the recent converts to parasols is Lee Se-jin, a 36-year-old consultant in Seoul. Though they were primarily seen as a feminine item just a few years ago, he said, in heat like this, such notions of gender have largely gone out the window.

“These days it really doesn’t feel strange to use a parasol as a man,” Mr. Lee said. “It’s been the biggest difference-maker in terms of actual cooling benefits.”

Kiuko Notoya contributed reporting and Li You contributed research.

item.title: How Social Media Spurred a Refugee Crisis Between Spain and Morocco
item.description:
Two days before tens of thousands of migrants surged into Ceuta, one of Spain’s enclaves on Morocco’s northern coast, a newspaper there posted a video on TikTok and Instagram showing two young women walking in the city in wet suits, their hair still damp.

The posts didn’t say so explicitly, but the implication was clear: The women had just swum across the border from Morocco. “Ceuta can’t take it anymore,” the newspaper, El Faro de Ceuta, declared in the posts.

On the other side of the border, the video resonated very differently. Cropped and reposted in Arabic, the video seemed like an invitation. The women were smiling, flashing peace signs and thumbs up and, most of all, walking around freely.

The video seemed to legitimize rumors that had percolated for weeks on social media suggesting that a recent ruling by Spain’s Supreme Court meant migrants who arrived illegally by sea could stay in the country. As one account on Facebook put it, falsely, “Ceuta is turning into an open gate,” when in fact migrants still faced expulsion after a judicial review.

The responses to the posts about the swimmers were a critical part of a cascade of disinformation that experts described as one of the starkest instances in which social media contributed directly to a real-world tragedy.

On July 30, tens of thousands of people, many spurred by unwarranted faith in the claims circulating online, poured into Ceuta in a human surge that overwhelmed the authorities on both sides of the border. About 90 people died, most of them by drowning, inflaming an already contentious debate in Europe and beyond over illegal migration and the economic and social factors that drive it.

“It started off as a din,” said Moustafa Ayad, a researcher with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, an international organization that tracks threats online, referring to the discussion online, “and then it avalanched.”

For nearly three weeks, millions of posts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, TikTok and Telegram speculated about how the Spanish court’s ruling had enhanced the chances of reaching Spanish territory, according to Mr. Ayad and other researchers who have studied what triggered the events that day.

The content appeared to spread organically, tapping into a seething desperation of many in Morocco and other parts of Africa to seek economic opportunities in Europe. That desperation was then exploited by online groups that organize human smuggling, which made offers on Facebook and WhatsApp to help those considering crossing.

The posts accelerated late last month as an increasing but still small number of people attempted the swim around the physical barriers that extend into the sea at the southern edge Ceuta, just north of the Moroccan town of Fnideq. Images of those who succeeded only seemed to encourage more people to act.

It is unclear whether the authorities in Spain and Morocco — or the platforms themselves — were aware of the groundswell online or raised any red flags about it by the afternoon of July 30, when, for reasons still not entirely clear, the number of people trying to cross the frontier suddenly exploded.

At least 215 accounts on Facebook that day posted the same exact message about the Supreme Court’s ruling, claiming incorrectly that no one who swam to Ceuta or another Spanish enclave on the Moroccan coast, Melilla, would be expelled, according to Maldita.es, a research organization in Spain.

The repetition suggested a coordinated effort to spread the information, which was subsequently shared by seemingly unwitting users.

One of the most prominent accounts to share the post, according to Maldita, belonged to Youssef Belhaissi, a spokesman for Morocco’s Inter-ministerial Delegation for Human Rights, a government agency in Rabat, the country’s capital. (Mr. Belhaissi, who has 1.3 million Facebook followers, did not respond to a request for comment).

Rumors have long shaped how migrants settle on routes abroad, which are fraught with unpredictable risks. Social media has accelerated the process, said Jorgen Carling, a migration expert at the Peace Research Institute Oslo.

“Even if the Supreme Court decision was inconsequential,” he said, “it gave the rumors that kernel of truth that made them much more trustworthy.”

Some of the shadowy groups on Facebook and WhatsApp that have previously offered to help smuggle people to Europe had more than 100,000 followers. Several used variations of the Arabic word for “burners,” harraga, slang for people who cross borders illegally.

One Facebook group linked to a group on WhatsApp that called itself “the path to Ceuta” with an emoji of a swimmer.

The groups offered advice, maps, equipment and even rides to towns abutting the border, the researchers found. Spain’s Ministry of the Interior claimed in a statement that “human trafficking networks” were “exploiting a court ruling to encourage the flow of undocumented migrants, mostly young people.”

Some of the groups appeared to be administered by people using telephone numbers from Algeria, but no evidence has emerged that any state played a role, the researchers said.

“You could see these calls to action — and they were handling logistics — more focused on trying to monetize the situation than acting as something organized by a government or a foreign power,” said Marcelino Madrigal, an expert on disinformation in Spain who documented the evolution of the content online. “The groups there were meant for coordination, as if we wanted to organize a march.”

In a statement, Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, said it had established a team to monitor the crisis in Ceuta as it unfolded and had removed “content that violates our policies — including content that offers to provide, facilitate or seek human smuggling services.”

Some accounts remain active and have, since the tragedy, turned into message boards for those desperate to learn the fate of loved ones who had not returned after the surge.

“This is my father, he has been missing since Thursday and there is no news,” one post said, sharing a photograph and a telephone number in Morocco if anyone had information.

From the start, misrepresentations of the Supreme Court’s ruling, which involved a case of a migrant who swam to Ceuta, laid the groundwork for the crisis. Under Spanish law, the authorities can immediately expel anyone who tries to breach a physical barrier to enter the country, but the court found that those who have not breached a barrier — say, by swimming in open water — would be subject to a judicial review.

The ruling was issued in late June and made public on July 8. In online discussions in Morocco, the nuances were lost. Over time, like a game of telephone, the ruling was portrayed as a significant reversal of Spain’s immigration laws, when in fact anyone who entered would still face expulsion if he or she could not substantiate a claim for refugee status.

The videos of the two young women swimmers were seen more than 32 million times, according to Marouane Lamharzi Alaoui, a co-founder of Firassa AI, a company that analyzes visual content. By contrast, a post on TikTok in French that sought to correct the record about the supposed border opening was viewed fewer than 2,000 times, he noted.

“I saw videos on Instagram that said: They will help you, they won’t send you back,” one of those who crossed said in a telephone interview. He spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his first name and his patronymic, Achraf Ben Ahmed.

Traveling by train from central Morocco, he said, he swam 12 kilometers, or almost eight miles, to Ceuta on July 29 after buying a wet suit and fins.

Within days of the surge of crossings, most of those who arrived in Ceuta returned to Morocco. Some remained, including Achraf, who said he was hiding in a forested part of Ceuta, venturing into town only to buy food. He still hopes to reach Europe after three previous unsuccessful attempts.

“I hope God facilitates things for us,” he said.

In the aftermath, some have questioned whether the groundswell online should have raised alarms. Mr. Madrigal blamed “the lack of responsibility from governments” and “insolence of platforms” that fail to monitor the content they spread.

“Nobody is responsible here,” he went on, referring to Mark Zuckerberg, the chief executive of Meta.

“Mr. Zuckerberg? The Moroccan government? The Spanish government?” Mr. Madrigal said. “If we haven’t identified that, it can happen again.”

Tiffany Hsu contributed reporting.

item.title: France Bans Unsolicited Telemarketing Calls
item.description:
In France, incessant cold calls advertising solar panels, roofs, heat pumps and other items will stop on Tuesday, when a ban on unsolicited telemarketing calls goes into effect.

Companies will no longer be allowed to advertise goods and services through such calls unless consumers previously gave their consent or if the calls are about a pre-existing contract.

The ban is unlikely to be met with any opposition in a country where 97 percent of the population say they are annoyed by daily telemarketing calls, which have been steadily increasing in recent years, according to a parliamentary report.

A leading consumer advocacy group, Que Choisir Ensemble, called the ban a “historic measure” that “should finally put an end to the daily harassment that the French have endured for far too long.”

“Peace and quiet is a right,” the group’s president, Marie-Amandine Stévenin, said in a statement. “This observation holds true both online and on the street, where we are inundated with calls to consume.”

Frédéric Billon, the head of Fédération de la Vente Directe, a business organization, said that the law would add administrative burdens for all local businesses that used to call their customers without giving it much thought.

“Today, that ‘without giving it much thought’ approach no longer exists,” he said. “You’ll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you’ll also have to keep proof of that consent.”

Mr. Billon also said he was worried about unfair competition from unethical companies operating within and outside France.

In Morocco, where France represents a major market for telemarketing companies, the ban could lead to the disappearance of up to 50,000 jobs in the country, according to a government official quoted by Le Matin, a daily Moroccan newspaper.

Delphine Batho, a French lawmaker, said in a broadcast interview on Monday that calls from abroad “will be illegal” and that “necessary steps must be taken, including with telecom operators, to ensure that these calls, which are scams, are technically blocked.”

The new legislation, which Parliament adopted in May last year, is a significant shift from having French people consent by default to receiving telemarketing calls. Previously, consumers could be contacted at random unless they signed up on “Bloctel,” a free government registry to avoid getting such calls.

Though phone numbers listed on “Bloctel” nearly doubled between 2021 and 2024 and more than 38 million calls a day were being blocked, the service was deemed inefficient because companies often failed to take it into account, according to the parliamentary report.

Under earlier legislation that aimed to tackle the issue, some companies in specific industries like home renovations for older people or for people with disabilities were already forbidden to make unsolicited telemarketing calls.

Now, individuals face a fine of up to 75,000 euros, or $87,000, and companies can be fined €375,000, or $433,000, if they fail to comply with the new law. For calls targeting vulnerable individuals, the sentence could be as much as five years in prison and a fine of €500,000, or $578,000.

“From a legislative standpoint, we couldn’t do any better,” Pierre-Jean Verzelen, the French senator behind the initial bill, said in a broadcast interview at the time the new ban was adopted in 2025.

“The government will have to act immediately, hitting companies that don’t play by the rules hard and fast,” he said. “That’s the price we’ll have to pay to get results.”

In a July decree specifying the application of the law, the government said that even if consumers agreed to receive cold calls, they could change their mind at any point and businesses would have to seek consent again within a year.

item.title: In a Sweltering Summer, These Italians Want Romans to Curl
item.description:
Taking a sweaty summer stroll past Rome’s ancient monuments, the last thing that the doctor Luca Puzziferri expected to find facing the Colosseum in July was a decidedly winter sport.

But there it was, a curling rink perched on the Oppian Hill, as this area overlooking the first-century amphitheater has been known since ancient times. Soon, Dr. Puzziferri was gleefully throwing stones with his wife and two friends during Italy’s third blistering heat wave in months.

“The whole thing was totally spontaneous, and we had so much fun,” said Dr. Puzziferri, 37, who lives in Rome.

His friend, Giuseppe Nicoletti, a 36-year-old programmer visiting from southern Italy, said he had enjoyed “dabbling” in curling after watching this year’s Winter Olympics, which Italy hosted.

“But I can say that it seems much easier from home,” he said, laughing. “I mean we’re really doing terribly.”

Italy’s curling team thrilled supporters, winning a bronze medal in the mixed doubles, boosting television ratings and inspiring sports officials to install the Oppian Hill rink in June, in the hopes that Romans would come out and play. Despite the heat.

“After the Olympics everyone had a dream: to experience what it was like to curl, and we enjoyed making that dream a reality,” said Diego Nepi Molineris, the managing director of Sport e Salute, the state-owned company behind the project.

The rinks were placed “at an iconic location, perhaps the most iconic in Italy, facing the Colosseum,” he said, to show that even a sport that many “label as minor can become magnificent.” (The rinks are also next to a skatepark that Roman officials boast has the best view in the world.)

“We believe that every sport is great, and it’s us who make it seem minor,” Mr. Nepi Molineris added.

To be fair, this isn’t a regulation rink. There is no ice, for one: The surface is high-density plastic. It’s also about 40 feet long by almost 10 feet wide, while a standard “sheet” — as the curling surface is known — is around 150 feet long and 16 feet wide. The stones weigh about a tenth of the regulation weight, and brooms are used to recover the stones rather than sweep a path for them to travel.

“It’s the idea of the game,” said Andrea Gios, president of the Italian Federation of Ice Sports, which supported the initiative. At the rink, people described playing as a mix between bowling and bocce, the bull’s-eye ballgame ubiquitous to Italian communities around the world. “It’s simpatico,” Mr. Gios said.

Carlo Scarpato, 24, one of the employees managing the rink, said his job consisted mostly of warning people not to step on the lubricated sheet so they wouldn’t slip and get hurt. “We also explain the basic rules of the game,” he added.

There were no time limits to how long people could play, he said, though this summer’s blistering heat made for pretty short games. “I can assure you that if you’re playing for five minutes, the reflection of the white makes it unbearably hot,” he said of the rink’s surface.

Curling was invented in the 16th century by Scottish farmers who played on frozen bogs, using smooth stones found in channels. Scottish immigrants imported the game to Canada, where the first club opened in 1807, followed by a club in the United States some 25 years later.

The sport is a relatively new entry to Italy, where curling only took root during the 1950s when a hotel owner installed a rink in Cortina d’Ampezzo — the Alpine Italian town that co-hosted this year’s Olympics. Many celebrities, including Brigitte Bardot, gave it a whirl.

But climate was never on Italy’s side. Currently, there are only seven dedicated curling rinks in Italy, all in the north, and 425 card-carrying curlers. “It’s a niche sport,” said Valentino Masotti, a curler who has written a book about it. By comparison, Canada has more than two million curlers who play at least once a year, “by a wide margin, the greatest number of curlers in the world,” according to Al Cameron, a spokesman for Curling Canada.

Since Mr. Gios became president of the ice sports federation 12 years ago, its investment in curling grew from 150,000 euros a year to 911,000 euros (about $171,000 to $1 million), and the sport was placed on more professional footing. In Italy, public funds to sports are allocated according to results, so the better players do, the more money the sport receives.

The meteoric rise of the tennis star Jannik Sinner, for instance, has quadrupled the funds given to tennis in just three years. But ice sports still don’t have a national reach.

“There are few facilities, so it’s hard to capitalize on the visibility you might get during the Olympic Games, where everyone goes crazy for curling and falls in love with the sport,” said Joël Retornaz, the captain of the Italian men’s Olympic team. “But then, if they actually want to try it, they struggle because it’s hard to find an arena.”

He said he was one of “lucky few” to have been born in the northern village of Cembra, in Trentino, where most locals start curling as children.

There are no curling arenas in central or southern Italy — at least not regulation ones — said Aldo Tuba, who runs an ice arena just outside Rome. After the Olympics, he received many calls expressing interest in curling, he said, so he cobbled together an improvised game using beer barrels instead of stones.

“It was entertaining,” he said, if unconventional. Now, Mr. Tuba is working with regional officials to drum up funds for a curling rink in his arena.

“As a European capital, Rome deserves a curling rink,” said Bianca Di Tommasi, president of the ice sports federation for the Lazio region. But she admitted that the increase in energy costs since the start of the Iran war had added financial challenges to opening one.

Mr. Nepi Molineris, the Sport e Salute official, said that if there was a demand, the rink at the Colosseum would be rebuilt using real ice come November. “Even if the ice won’t be perfect for an international competition, it will be perfect for national entertainment,” he said.

On a recent Saturday, the heat didn’t deter a gaggle of sporty teens visiting Italy for an international basketball camp. They were captivated, playing through the heat, squealing and cheering as their coaches looked on.

“It’s a lot of fun, especially to do in front of the Colosseum,” said Zia Gonzales, 21, who coaches girls in the United States.

“I’m glad we did this at the end of the camp and not the start,” added Shaun Hoyle, 29, who coaches boys in Britain. “Otherwise we may have lost them here.”

item.title: What to Know About the Cuban Mafia in Quintana Roo
item.description:
For years, luxury boats and marine equipment were going missing from southwest Florida cities, from Sarasota to Naples to Marco Island.

Even after three South Florida men were arrested in January 2010 in Sarasota in a sting to trap thieves stealing GPS devices, it would take a decade for federal authorities to link those cases to a major conspiracy that trafficked people and stolen vessels between Cuba, Mexico and the United States.

It became the focus of an F.B.I. and Homeland Security Investigations task force known as Operation Sisyphus. Eventually Raúl G. Rodríguez Castro, a grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, was named as someone who helped the Quintana Roo mafia from inside Cuba, though he has not been charged.

In 2020, the U.S. Department of Justice indicted several Cubans based in Mexico suspected of being members of a criminal group known as the Cuban Mafia in Quintana Roo, a state in eastern Mexico. They were accused of stealing boats in southwest Florida as far back as 2009 and using them to smuggle thousands of migrants out of Cuba to Mexico and ultimately the United States.

Among the migrants smuggled were professional baseball players, including shortstop Adeiny Hechavarría, who played for a variety of teams, and Los Angeles Dodgers slugger Yasiel Puig.

About 25 people died during the voyages, according to court documents.

Migrants who were trafficked and could not pay the $10,000 smuggling fee were held captive in Mexico, tortured with Tasers, and their families were extorted, prosecutors said. Some women were forced to work in strip clubs, according to court records.

The traffickers would contact the victims’ relatives and threaten to torture, starve and kill their victims if the relatives refused to pay, the U.S. Department of Justice said. Those who paid the fee were sent by bus to the U.S.-Mexico border and coached on how to request political asylum.

“We would do physical punishment,” one of the traffickers, Reynaldo Crespo Márquez, testified in 2023 after pleading guilty in U.S. federal court in Miami. “Sometimes they were beaten up with a wooden board or with a Taser gun.”

Among other schemes prosecutors discovered: buying goods with stolen credit cards and smuggling them into Cuba for sale at Cuban government stores. The defendants were also charged with stealing more than 600 outboard boat engines and vessels from the Tampa area and shipping them to the migrant smugglers in Quintana Roo.

“These guys were the real pirates of the Caribbean,” said David Bolton, a veteran private investigator who said he stumbled upon the operation while working on an unrelated case and brought the issue to federal authorities.

He described the members as “ruthless killers.”

In 2009, several group members conspired to kidnap and kill a man in a dispute involving a Mexican cartel called the Zetas. His body was dismembered and disposed of at sea, according to court documents.

Members of the organization also sought to profit from drug trafficking and fraud schemes, which included smuggling boats, cars and trucks, the Justice Department said. Some boats were sold to pay off foreign officials or used as bribes, documents show.

At least six co-defendants pleaded guilty, including José Miguel González Vidal, 38.

Mr. González Vidal later said he gave a boat to Mr. Rodríguez Castro, former Cuban president Raúl Castro’s grandson, court records show.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security called Mr. González Vidal “a career criminal” whose criminal record included multiple convictions for false imprisonment, robbery, grand theft, larceny and illegal use of credit cards. He illegally entered the United States at least twice, Homeland Security said.

A dual Cuban-Spanish citizen, he had been deported to Spain only to be extradited back to Florida to face federal RICO conspiracy charges.

He pleaded guilty in late 2023 and was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Court records show a federal judge recently sealed his closed case, which is sometimes done when a defendant is cooperating with prosecutors. His lawyer, Juan D. Berrios, declined to comment.

The Cuban government called the accusations involving Mr. Rodríguez Castro “slander,” and Mr. Rodríguez Castro did not respond to requests for comment.

The defendant who Mr. Crespo Márquez had testified against, Javier Hernández, of Miami Beach, was found guilty for his role in the conspiracy — largely smuggling boats to Mexico — and was sentenced to eight years in prison.

In April, Mexican authorities announced they had arrested a key financier of the Quinta Roo group, Remigio Valdez-Lao, 59, who is expected to face extradition. The New York Times was unable to determine whether Mr. Valdez-Lao was represented by a lawyer.

Mr. Valdez-Lao’s name had surfaced before: he was among those arrested in 2010 in Sarasota.

item.title: What We Know About the Earthquake in Colombia
item.description:
A major earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, killing more than 100 people, damaging hundreds of buildings in the country’s west and prompting a frantic search for survivors.

The 7.4-magnitude earthquake was the most powerful recorded in the South American nation in the past decade, the Colombian Geological Survey said.

President Abelardo De La Espriella of Colombia, who had been sworn into office just three days before the quake, declared a state of emergency and said that he would directly lead the disaster response.

Here’s what to know.

The epicenter of the quake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, was about three miles east of San José del Palmar — a town of about 5,000 people in the Chocó region, one of the poorest parts of Colombia.

The temblor, which struck about 7:34 a.m. local time, rattled much of the country, though the impact was worst in cities and towns in the foothills of the Andes.

Major damage was reported in Cali, the country’s third-largest city, which has about two million residents. The cities of Pereira and Manizales, hubs of Colombia’s coffee-growing region that are each home to about 500,000 people, were also badly hit.

The country’s two largest cities — Bogotá, the capital, and Medellín — appeared to have escaped the worst of the damage. But residents there and across the country reported intense shaking.

The quake was also felt in neighboring countries including Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela, though there were no reports of serious damage.

The earthquake killed at least 111 people and injured 87 others, according to Mr. De La Espriella. The death toll was expected to rise as rescuers and residents dug through rubble.

Rescue efforts were underway across western Colombia. In Cali, Mayor Alejando Eder said that emergency workers were focusing on finding people in debris from 10 collapsed buildings. Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán of Bogotá said the city was preparing to send rescue crews to hard-hit cities.

It is unclear how long people can survive trapped in rubble after an earthquake, researchers say. But some experts say that there is a 72-hour “golden” window in which the most lives can be saved.

The quake damaged at least 1,575 homes, 18 health centers and 52 schools, Mr. De La Espriella said.

In Cali, at least 26 buildings collapsed, trapping people inside, according to its mayor. In Calima El Darién, a town north of Cali, a hospital collapsed and another was overwhelmed with victims.

There was also widespread damage, including piles of rubble from collapsed buildings, in Pereira and Manziales. Several airports in western Colombia, including in Pereira and Manziales, were among the structures damaged, according to the Colombian Civil Aviation Authority.

The agency said it had suspended operations at some airports until structural damage could be assessed.

The earthquake is the first big test for Mr. De La Espriella, a right-wing former lawyer with no previous political experience who was sworn in on Friday after winning the presidential election in June.

He said in a video posted on social media on Monday that he had canceled his travel plans to head to Bogotá, where he said he would “personally assume leadership” of the emergency response.

“You’re not alone,” he wrote, addressing people affected by the disaster. “The state is present and taking action.”

item.title: Syrian Court Sentences Bashar al-Assad to Death in Absentia for War Crimes
item.description:
A court in Syria sentenced Bashar al-Assad, the country’s ousted president, and several other former government officials to death in absentia on Tuesday after convicting them of committing murder, torture and crimes against humanity during a nearly 14-year civil war.

The verdicts marked the end of the first trial related to the war held in Syria since Mr. al-Assad was overthrown in December 2024, and they were met with celebrations inside and outside the courthouse in Damascus, the capital.

Eight other people were sentenced, including Maher al-Assad, Mr. al-Assad’s younger brother, who led an elite army unit that was instrumental in attacking and killing opponents of the regime throughout the war.

Atef Najib, a cousin of Mr. al-Assad and the former political security chief in the southern province of Daraa, was also convicted and sentenced to death. He was the only defendant present during the trial.

After the regime fell, Mr. al-Assad and many of his family members and officials, including Maher, fled to Russia, which granted him political asylum. The Syrian government has called for him to be extradited to Syria, but Russian authorities are unlikely to return him.

Syria’s new interim government has sought to achieve some measure of justice for crimes committed by Mr. al-Assad and his regime during the brutal civil war.

But Syrians have become increasingly resentful and impatient at the lack of accountability. Some have accused the interim government of not prioritizing that search for justice, given the pace of trials.

International legal experts, however, have cautioned that transitional justice takes time and cannot be rushed.

At the court in Damascus, after the verdict was announced, the families of some of the victims — some of whom carried photos of their deceased loved ones — chanted “With our souls, with our blood, we sacrifice ourselves for the martyrs.”

Mr. Najib was head of the security branch in Daraa when the revolt against Mr. al-Assad started in 2011. After teenagers painted graffiti on the side of a school there, suggesting that Mr. al-Assad would be the next dictator to fall in the Arab Spring protests that were sweeping the Middle East at the time, they were arrested and tortured.

When protests erupted in response, the government responded with deadly gunfire, sparking mass demonstrations across the country that eventually grew into an armed uprising.

Mr. Najib was responsible for those killings, as well as torture, arbitrary detentions, and the deadly suppression of the protests, the Syrian court ruled.

Last year, the Syrian government formed by the rebels who ousted Mr. al-Assad established a National Commission for Transitional Justice. The head of the commission, Abdul Basit Abdul Latif, said on Tuesday that the verdict against Mr. Najib was an important step toward justice.

item.title: Spain’s Complex Ties With Morocco Fuel Speculation Over Ceuta Migrant Surge
item.description:
The actor Javier Bardem wondered if Israel had something to do with the rush of over 70,000 migrants last month from Morocco to Spain. Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Republican congresswoman and veteran conspiracy theorist, suggested the Republican Party was behind it. Others said King Mohammed VI of Morocco had set off the crisis to mess with Spain.

Experts have said that there is no evidence that any state played a role in masterminding the unprecedented migration to Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa. The Spanish and Moroccan governments blamed the surge, which killed about 90 migrants before most of the people involved had retreated to Morocco, on a viral social media misinformation campaign by smugglers.

But that hasn’t stopped all sorts of conjecture about what really happened. That speculation is partly rooted, analysts said, in the deeply complicated relationship between Spain and Morocco.

Spain occupied parts of Morocco for much of the 20th century, and many Moroccans still contest Spain’s control over its African territories, including Ceuta. Yet, the two countries are also interdependent for intricate economic, political and geopolitical reasons.

They have conflicting positions on Algeria, Israel and the Trump administration. Spain has a fraught relationship with Washington and Jerusalem, but a warming one with Algiers. Morocco, however, sees Algeria as a rival but is improving ties with Israel and the United States.

People of all ideological stripes have seized on all those layers of complexity to develop the mystery, or conspiracy, of their choosing.

“We are seeing the simplification of a very complex reality,” said Pol Morillas, director of the Barcelona Center for International Affairs, an independent research organization. “This is where all the different theories come in.”

In an era of rising nationalism and misinformation, Mr. Morillas said, the Ceuta situation fed the wildest of imaginations. “It’s a sign of the times,” he said.

For the most part, Mr. Morillas added, the Spain-Morocco relationship is managed smoothly. Spain is Morocco’s main trading partner in Europe. Morocco also accounts for the largest source of legal migrants to Spain. It also usually prevents unauthorized migrants from reaching Spain, even if it has in the past, experts say, weaponized migrant flows for geopolitical benefit.

In 1975, as the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco lay on his deathbed, Morocco sensed weakness and sent 350,000 people, as well as military forces, into the Western Sahara territory that Spain had controlled for nearly a century. The move, known as the Green March, helped to prompt Spain to withdraw.

“Quite a few people in Ceuta are already comparing it with the Green March,” said Enrique Avila, a retired political scientist in Ceuta who served as an artillery soldier for Spain in the Western Sahara during the withdrawal. “You feel threatened, and it is constant.”

In Spain’s absence, a conflict escalated in the Western Sahara between Algerian-backed separatists, who supported self-determination for its residents, and Morocco, which argued that it had a historical claim to the lands. Spain, seeking functional relations with both Algeria and Morocco, remained neutral.

In 2020, the Trump administration, helped persuade Morocco to normalize its relations with Israel in exchange for American recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Israel later did the same.

Spain refused to follow their example, even allowing a separatist leader to be treated for the coronavirus in a Spanish hospital.

It was amid those heightened tensions in 2021 that Morocco loosened border controls and let about 10,000 migrants cross the border into Ceuta. Many in Spain saw the move as a clear geopolitical flex to punish Spain for its neutrality on Western Sahara.

A year later, Spain reversed its position and backed Moroccan control over the territory — pleasing Morocco but angering Algeria, the separatists’ backer.

This year, Spanish leaders tried to improve ties with Algeria, hoping to import more Algerian gas but potentially antagonizing Morocco.

On July 20, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez traveled for the first time in four years to Algeria for talks to improve relations. The surge from Morocco happened days later.

The confluence of events was, for some, proof enough of a Moroccan plot, even as Moroccan experts cautioned that such a deadly disaster was unlikely to have been orchestrated by the kingdom.

“It’s hard to believe this caught the authorities completely by surprise,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the leader of Ceuta’s government, said recently when asked if he thought Morocco had had a hand in the surge. “You can’t hide 80,000 people in a trunk. I would have expected a movement of people on that scale to have been detected.”

Such doubts were amplified by the fact that Morocco has grown increasingly friendly with Israel and the United States, which have both had tense relationships with Spain recently.

Mr. Sánchez has clashed with President Trump over migration and Iran, as well as with Israel over its conduct in Gaza. By contrast, Morocco announced in July that it would name a major highway after Mr. Trump, and it has been talking publicly about helping to secure Gaza.

Then, as the Ceuta crisis unraveled, Israeli officials appeared to relish Spain’s discomfort.

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, took a dig at the Spanish government by asking why Spain had criticized Israeli actions in Gaza when it has a colonial legacy of its own.

“Maybe before it continues lecturing us,” Mr. Danon wrote on social media, “it’s time it explained to the world why it still maintains colonial enclaves in Africa.”

That appeared to have fueled speculation from some of Mr. Sánchez’s own allies, who now seemed to think something big was going down. On July 31, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, seized on Mr. Danon’s post as evidence of, well, something.

“Well,” Mr. Puente wrote, “it’s all starting to become quite clear.”

When asked by The Times to explain what had become clear, Mr. Puente forwarded government talking points that contradicted the idea of a state-led conspiracy.

Still, similar doubts simmered across the Spanish left. “The Moroccan dictatorship, in the service of the U.S. and Israel, is once again blackmailing Spain and Europe this summer by turning its own people into disposable cannon fodder,” wrote Gabriel Rufián, a prominent member of the Spanish Parliament.

Irene Montero, the former leader of the far-left party Podemos, wrote on social media, “If you pay a dictatorship like Morocco to do the dirty work, when Morocco wants more — or when the US and Israel order them to — they stop doing it to blackmail you.”

The post was shared by Mr. Bardem, one of Spain’s most celebrated actors and a vocal critic of Israel’s war in Gaza.

Figures from the American far-right made similar claims.

Ms. Taylor Greene seized on a recent congressional report, connected to a House bill, that recommended $40 million in security assistance to Morocco. The report, produced by a Republican-led committee, referred to Ceuta as a “Spanish-administered” land “located in Moroccan territory.”

That was enough for Ms. Taylor Greene to conclude in a post on X: “Republicans paid $40 MILLION of your tax dollars to Morocco to invade Spain.”

There is no evidence for any of those theories.

But the “increased chaos” in the world, coupled with Morocco’s strategy of “calculated ambiguity,” had made everything seem plausible, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, director of the Center for Contemporary Arab Studies in Madrid.

“Was this planned? Was this orchestrated?” he asked. “So many different layers.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting from Ceuta, Spain, and Madrid, and Aaron Boxerman from Jerusalem.

item.title: The Eclipse Is Coming, and Iceland Is Looking for a Break in the Clouds
item.description:
A total solar eclipse will cast a shadow across several European countries on Wednesday. But in Iceland, where eclipse chasers were hoping for one of the best possible views, the unpredictable weather may prove to be a spoiler.

So many Icelanders — and some intrepid visitors — plan to make a game-day decision about where to go to watch the spectacle.

“It’s the worst country to watch an eclipse,” said Margret Brynjolfsdottir, who lives in Iceland’s remote northwest, part of the narrow band of the globe where the moon will completely block out the sun.

As of Tuesday, forecasters were predicting overcast skies and rain across most of Iceland. Ms. Brynjolfsdottir, a physical therapist, planned to watch the eclipse from home, no matter how the sky looks. But Icelanders are used to fickle weather, and many are likely to check the forecast on Wednesday morning and hit the road to find the clearest skies they can.

In short, no one really knows where anyone is going to go.

“We are as prepared as we can be,” said Birna Mjoll Atladottir, who runs the westernmost hotel in Iceland, Hotel Breidavik. The period when the moon completely eclipses the sun — known as totality — will last an impressive two minutes and 10 seconds at her hotel. (Just up the road, on the cliffs at the edge of the country, it will stretch on for another three seconds.)

Ms. Atladottir has cleared two fields around her hotel, erected 10 new portable toilets and ordered a month’s worth of food.

If the weather cooperates, she could get flooded with campers. But if not, all that expensive preparation could be for naught.

“We don’t know anything,” she said, sighing.

This will be Europe’s first total solar eclipse since 1999. On most of the continent, the moon will obscure only a portion of the sun, but parts of Russia, Greenland, Spain and Portugal as well as Iceland are in the path of the total eclipse. (People in Spain will be trying to stay safe in extreme heat.)

That rare moment of darkness will last longer here in the Westfjords, a remote region of northwestern Iceland, than almost anywhere else, excluding the oceans. The Westfjords, which are not on Iceland’s main tourist route, has been gearing up to host the eclipse enthusiasts (also known as umbraphiles, or people who love the shadows).

Visitors began making reservations years ago. Some Airbnb hosts and hotel owners have jacked up their prices; some rooms that usually cost a few hundred dollars are going for thousands.

“Iceland is pretty much sold out,” said Saevar Helgi Bragason, a science communicator who has become the country’s unofficial eclipse czar.

And in recent months, harried officials in the Westfjords and elsewhere have been scrambling to fix roads, boost mobile coverage and reserve the country’s relatively few portable toilets.

Foreign tourists aren’t the main concern, officials said. That’s because most of the roughly 75,000 foreigners set to be in Iceland that day have probably committed to a fixed plan.

Instead, it’s the Icelanders, who are used to spending their summers chasing the sun. Any number of the island’s 400,000 residents — about a third of whom will not be able to see a total eclipse from their homes — could set out to find the best possible view. That could result in gridlock on unpaved, less-traveled rural roads.

“The Icelandic weather doesn’t really allow you to make plans ahead of time,” said Diego Ragnar Angemi, an amateur astronomer who lives in the northwestern corner of the Westfjords, where totality is set to last for some 90 seconds.

Conditions can differ from fjord to fjord, Mr. Angemi said, so even a short drive can change the view completely. “I am going to stay home only if I see that it’s cloudy from here to Reykjavik,” he said.

If there’s sunshine anywhere nearby, he said, “I will take the chance — of course.”

The Westfjords have mostly been spared Iceland’s crush of tourists in megabuses, who come to gaze at the northern lights, soak in hot tubs and pose with hot dogs.

This is the rare unbeaten path. And it shows.

Green hills, unmarked by houses, slope up from the fjords. Phone calls drop as you drive around bends. Big grocery stores are hours away. The biggest village in the southern Westfjords, Patreksfjordur, has about 700 residents, four restaurants, a gas station and a liquor store.

Driving here can be, at best, bumpy. Many roads that lace across fjords are unpaved, pitted with potholes deep enough to chatter even a clenched jaw.

On a normal day, that wouldn’t be a major problem. These aren’t busy roads — a quarter of an hour can pass without another car being seen. Most people know to take it slow.

“But it’s not a normal day,” said Johann B. Skulason, a national police official who is helping to coordinate the work of different agencies as Iceland prepares for the eclipse. He spoke from a command center in Reykjavik that would normally be used for a crisis like a volcanic eruption.

Road crews in the Westfjords have been leveling gravel roads, like the one that stretches out past Hotel Breidavik — Ms. Atladottir’s hotel — toward the western Latrabjarg cliffs, where puffins roost and thousands of eclipse chasers could soon gather.

The crews were cutting it close. On Saturday evening, hours after the first people arrived to pitch a tent outside Hotel Breidavik, workers were laying new gravel.

A nearby hospital and fire department have been staffing up and preparing to send emergency crews out to the cliffs. Telecom companies have been strengthening networks for months. And there may never be a better day for Iceland’s waste management industry.

Jon Thorir Frantzson, the chief executive of the Icelandic Container Association, a private company, said all of his portable toilets — he has about 250 — have been rented for months. “It’s never been like this,” he said.

“It’s crazy to have them there, in the middle of nowhere,” he added. “Dragging them all to the Westfjords? That has never happened.”

Ms. Atladottir got her first booking for this Wednesday 14 years ago. She first thought it was a joke. Who makes a booking so far in advance?

Now, it’s all too real. Her rooms have long been booked, but there was still plenty of space for campers. On Saturday, her phone kept ringing.

“I would like to know if we can make a reservation for the 12th?” a caller asked, the second inquiry in under an hour.

Ms. Atladottir calmly explained that no, they were not taking bookings for campsites, but yes, they had more than enough space.

The caller thanked her, and hung up.

“How are we going to be prepared?” Ms. Atladottir said, laughing. “Are we going to expect 100 people — or 1,000 people — or what?”

By Monday, more than a dozen people had already set up their tents in the field outside her hotel. Whatever happens, it’ll be magical, there on her remote stretch of beach, looking up as the sky darkens briefly into night.

Egill Bjarnason contributed reporting from Husavik, in northern Iceland.

item.title: ‘We Know They Are Coming’: A Syrian Holdout Province Fears Takeover
item.description:
Gunmen swept into southern Syria last year, setting off one of the deadliest bouts of sectarian violence in years.

This southern province, Sweida, is home to many in the Druse minority. Some are wary of the central government.

The sectarian violence killed hundreds of people, razed entire villages and displaced tens of thousands, officials said.

An armed standoff persists. For now, residents watch and wait, fearful that violence could erupt again.

Visuals by Nanna Heitmann

Text by Abdi Latif Dahir

The journalists made two trips to Sweida Province in Syria, speaking to displaced residents, political leaders, security officials and medical workers.

When Syria’s government forcibly took control this year of a northeastern region long dominated by the Kurdish minority, the Druse in Sweida watched with growing unease.

The Druse, who, like the Kurds, have for years controlled their own region, saw the writing on the wall.

“We know they are coming,” said Sumayah al-Yousef, 65, a Druse resident of Sweida who was among the people displaced last summer by the wave of sectarian violence. After days of clashes between local groups and the entry of government forces into the fighting, more than 1,700 people, most of them Druse, were killed, according to the United Nations.

Sweida is the only Syrian province that has not submitted to the authority of the central government, headed by former rebels who ousted the longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in late 2024. The government that replaced Mr. al-Assad initially struggled to extend its authority over all of Syria, then seemed to be turning a corner at the start of this year with its takeover of the Kurdish-led northeast.

Across much of Syria, the end of Mr. al-Assad’s rule has been greeted with relief and hopes that the country can finally reunite and move on after years of internecine war. Yet those hopes have been accompanied by questions about the new government and whether it can build a state that Syrians across the country trust.

Druse residents repeatedly told us — during two trips to Sweida Province in November and January, as well as in follow-up phone and text interviews in the months since — that it was only a matter of time before the government moved to assert control over the area.

We spoke to nearly two dozen civilians, civil servants, security officials, medical workers and religious leaders about the sectarian violence in Sweida last summer and its aftermath.

Varying interests complicate Sweida’s fate.

Syrian leaders say reunifying the country under one authority is necessary to restore order, bring stability and prevent further fragmentation after nearly 14 years of civil war.

Some Druse residents of Sweida fear the post-Assad authorities, whose leaders have roots in a group once linked to Al Qaeda and whose forces they accuse of carrying out massacres against them. Israel is also wary of Syrian government forces expanding their reach toward its border, concerned that the area could eventually become a launchpad for attacks.

Sweida Province stretches across rocky highlands roughly 60 miles southeast of the Syrian capital, Damascus, with stony fields and scattered orchards defining the landscape.

The Druse have called these uplands home for ages. Their faith emerged centuries ago as an offshoot of a branch of Shiite Islam, though many typically do not identify as Muslim today.

Driving to the province from Damascus, we passed through at least six government checkpoints set up on a desolate stretch of land. Villages along the route lie deserted, their charred remains a stark reminder of last summer’s violence.

In July 2025, skirmishes broke out between armed Bedouins, part of Syria’s Sunni majority, and Druse militias. The communities have long clashed over grazing land, property and access to water, disputes sharpened by sectarian divisions.

What began as localized fighting quickly escalated.

Government forces, along with allied fighters, descended on Sweida’s windswept highlands, killing civilians, destroying towns and villages and displacing tens of thousands, according to independent monitors and witnesses.

While the Druse bore the brunt of the violence, Druse fighters have also been accused in some of the killings last summer, according to activists and human rights groups. Some Druse leaders have denied or rejected responsibility for abuses or killings.

Syria’s Defense Ministry said last year that it was aware of “shocking and grave violations” committed in Sweida by “an unidentified group wearing military uniforms.”

A government body investigating the killings issued its final report in March and said there would be legal actions against some individuals, according to SANA, Syria’s state news agency. Some of the cases have been referred to a military court in Damascus, officials said.

The Syrian government’s effort to bring Sweida under its control is fraught in many ways, not least because of neighboring Israel’s keen interest in maintaining Druse control in Sweida.

Israel has a sizable Druse minority and has long cultivated close ties with the community, a relationship that extends to the Syrian Druse.

President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria has sought to project a more moderate image to the world, promising to protect minority rights and saying that Syria has no interest in fighting with neighbors or interfering in their internal affairs. Yet Israeli officials have voiced deep distrust of Syria’s leaders, some of whom have roots in extremist groups. They are also uneasy about the government extending its authority near its border, fearing it could become a staging ground for attacks on Israel.

After the clashes, Israel struck Syria’s Defense Ministry and an area near the presidential palace in Damascus. It also launched airstrikes against government forces in Sweida.

Israeli officials vowed to protect the Syrian Druse and demanded that the region remain demilitarized, without the Syrian Army or its allies deploying or operating in the area. At the time, Mr. al-Sharaa accused Israel of trying to sow “chaos” and undermining Syria’s unity.

“Israel stood with us,” Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, the Druse spiritual leader most vocal in welcoming Israeli support, said in an interview in January. “Israel was the first to extend a helping hand.”

Mr. al-Hijri likened the authorities in Damascus to their authoritarian predecessors, saying the government’s brutality persisted even as the faces changed. He said the Druse saw no future under Mr. al-Sharaa’s government and insisted that secession was the only viable option for Sweida.

His stance is more hard-line than some other Druse religious leaders, who have not publicly called for secession.

After days of clashes in July 2025, a cease-fire was announced between the Syrian government and armed Druse factions in Sweida.

It has barely held in the year since.

Snipers occasionally take aim at one another across olive orchards and peach trees. Clashes break out in villages along the front line between the National Guard, a 28,000-strong militia in Sweida loyal to Mr. al-Hijri, and government forces and their allies.

The Guard is in constant contact with Israel, said Talal Amer, its spokesman, though he did not specify the nature of that coordination.

At the center of the provincial capital, also known as Sweida, life seems to have slowed to a crawl. Construction sites are abandoned, and once-bustling shops and vegetable markets are cloaked in an uncanny hush.

In the year after the eruption of sectarian violence, Sweida officials and residents say the government has intensified its pressure on the region to submit to its authority. It has repeatedly cut electricity and water, damaged power lines and pipes during military operations and blocked aid groups from repairing them, they say.

Humanitarian aid, including lifesaving food and medical supplies, has often been delayed or restricted before reaching the provincial capital, according to residents and Druse officials.

Mustafa al-Bakkour, the regional governor appointed by Mr. al-Sharaa last year before the summer violence, denied the accusations. He said the government was still paying salaries, helping residents rebuild destroyed homes and allowing aid in regularly. He also accused local forces of deliberately cutting electricity to drive demand for solar energy systems they sell.

And he called Mr. al-Hijri and his associates “a gang with personal interests” who have no “interest for matters to be resolved.”

For now, many of those displaced remain trapped in shelters in Sweida city.

One of them is Sheikh Merhej Shahin, whose life, until last summer, was measured in farm work, prayer and routine. When gunmen stormed his village, Al Thaala, he said he realized that life as he knew it was over. The assailants, he said, beat him, shaved his mustache and left him for dead.

“It was only God’s grace that protected me,” he said.

He dreams of returning home, even as he remains with his ailing wife, who is struggling to get the medication she needs. Despite everything, he said, “We will not break.”
